summary: An excerpt from a novel (apparently Kate Douglas Wiggin's Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm) set at a graduation day. Rebecca and her friend Emma Jane say goodbye to childhood; Rebecca, the class president, leads her classmates to the church in a flower-decked haycart rather than marching in pairs. Adam Ladd, newly arrived from Portland, admires the scene and then hears a sob from a forlorn girl in white behind a hedge.
one_line: At a village graduation, Rebecca leads her classmates in a flower-decked haycart, and Adam Ladd notices a weeping girl behind a hedge.
key_facts: Rebecca and Emma Jane discuss the closing of the 'golden gates of childhood' and reference Maggie Tulliver in The Mill on the Floss.
Emma Jane says she would not care how the gates swung or clanged 'if only you and I were on the same side of the gate'.
Rebecca says her only sorrow is that Emmie is not graduating with her.
A message from Calvin arrives saying, "I'm lactose intolerant," and nothing more.
Adam Ladd had just arrived from Portland and was walking to the church when he stopped under a tree in the main street.
The class did not march two by two from the seminary to the church; they proceeded by royal chariot instead.
The vehicle was a haycart decked with green vines and bunches of long-stemmed field daisies, the class flower.
Two white horses pulled the cart, with flower-trimmed reins.
The twelve girls of the class sat in the floral bower on maple boughs, while the ten boys marched on either side wearing buttonhole bouquets of daisies.
Rebecca drove, seated on a green-covered bench that looked not unlike a throne.
Adam thought Rebecca might have been a young Muse or Sibyl, and the hayrack might have been painted as an allegorical picture of The Morning of Life.
Adam stood under the elms in the old village street where his mother had walked half a century earlier.
Adam heard a little sob from a forlorn person in white behind a hedge in a nearby garden.
